## The big picture

A pricing model is a machine. Feed it parameters and it returns a price. The trouble is that the parameters are **estimates**, and small changes in them can move the price a lot. Robust pricing replaces the single number with an **interval of prices**: the cheapest and the most expensive values consistent with everything we believe about the parameters.

## 1. Nonlinear affine processes

Affine models such as Vasicek, Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) and Heston are the workhorses of interest-rate and volatility modelling because their prices come in near closed form. Fadina, Neufeld & Schmidt (2019) showed how to keep that structure while letting the drift and volatility parameters move inside an **uncertainty set**. Prices then come from a *nonlinear* expectation, the worst or best case over all admissible parameter paths.

**Questions I work on:** how to estimate the uncertainty set from data, how to check the nonlinear Feller condition (which keeps rates positive), and how to compute the price bounds efficiently.

*Start here:* [Part 1](posts/01-cir-from-coin-flips/index.qmd) · Part 2 arrives December 15

## 2. Robust currency option pricing

A currency option depends on *two* interest rates (domestic and foreign) and on the exchange-rate volatility. My current project builds on the stochastic-volatility FX option literature, starting from Melino & Turnbull (1990, 1991), and recasts it in the nonlinear CIR framework. The goal is option price bounds that stay honest about parameter uncertainty.

*Blog posts on this:* Part 3 (January 15) and Part 6 (April 15)

## 3. Weather derivatives

Temperature-based contracts (heating and cooling degree-day options) protect farms, utilities and insurers against weather risk. Temperature models are mean-reverting and seasonal, and their parameters are very uncertain, which makes them a natural next application of the same robust machinery. *Blog post on this:* Part 4 (February 15).

## Methods and tools

Stochastic calculus · nonlinear (sublinear) expectations · HJB / Black–Scholes–Barenblatt PDEs · Fourier pricing (Gil-Pelaez inversion) · maximum-likelihood estimation with constraints · Python, R, MATLAB.
